A summary of changes to the Troy School District High-School Course Description Book (CDB) for the 2025/2026 school year. Five courses were added. Advanced Forensic Techniques and Ethical Practices (Science), grades 11-12, 1 semester, half credit, no retake, prerequisites Biology, Chemistry 1, and Forensic Science, covers crime scene reconstruction, additional trace evidence, impressions, toxicology, glass, toolmarks and ballistics analysis, DNA and blood analysis, and real-world dilemmas and case studies within forensic science and the criminal justice system. Creative Connections (Visual Art), grades 9-12, 1 semester, half credit, no prerequisite, brings general education and special education students together in a collaborative, inclusive art-making environment emphasizing empathy, communication, peer mentorship, and teamwork. Data Structures and Algorithms (Math), grades 10-12, 2 semesters, half credit per semester, prerequisite Geometry, is described (via Introduction to Data Science) as combining data analysis, computing, and mathematics through manipulating, visualizing, and analyzing real-world datasets. Graphic Novels (English), grades 11-12, 1 semester, half credit, no prerequisite, explores the combination of visual art and narrative storytelling, developing visual analysis skills, exploring diverse narratives, creating original graphic texts, and completing inquiry synthesis projects and rhetorical analysis writing. Course 005805 LEAP: Linking Education and People, grades 11-12, half credit per semester, retake allowed, prerequisite of being a LEAP leader, empowers upperclassmen as role models for freshmen and develops leadership skills in communication, organization, and problem solving.

Several name changes are listed: Achievement Skills becomes Integrated Studies; Accounting 1 becomes Financial Accounting 1; a second Accounting course becomes Financial Accounting 2 (the source text repeats 'Accounting 1'); Financial Management becomes Building Wealth and Investments; Mechatronics 1 becomes Engineering and Advanced Manufacturing; Mechatronics 2 becomes Engineering and Digital Manufacturing Systems; and Music Theory AP is redesigned and renamed Music Theory. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A suggested resolution presented as agenda item 10.A under 'Other' business at the Troy School District Board of Education regular meeting on February 25, 2025, urging the board to support the federal IDEA Full Funding Act.

The accompanying background explains that the K-12 Alliance of Michigan held a press conference to both celebrate the success of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) on the 50th anniversary of its passage and to press the federal government to finally fund it adequately. It states that Congress has never funded the program higher than 18%, and that this year funding has dropped back to 10.3%, costing Michigan roughly $650 million in a single year. Michigan school boards are being asked to pass a resolution in support of the IDEA Full Funding Act; signed resolutions will be shared with members of Congress at the K-12 Alliance symposium in April to demonstrate support and the need for action. The recommended action is acceptance of the resolution, which includes blank 'Moved By,' 'Supported By,' and 'Yes'/'No' lines for the vote.

The resolution's WHEREAS clauses assert that: public education is the cornerstone of democracy; in the decade following the Great Recession, students across the U.S. lost nearly $600 billion from states' disinvestment in public schools; both state and federal funding were already failing to meet student needs before the COVID-19 pandemic; since the pandemic, students have needed additional academic, social, emotional and mental-health support, personnel, professional development, technology and facility updates; research consistently shows increased education funding positively affects academic performance, graduation rates and future earnings; when IDEA was passed in 1975 the federal government committed to pay 40 percent of the average per-pupil expenditure for special education; that financial pledge has never been met and is currently funded at approximately 10.7 percent, leaving a gap of billions of dollars; Troy School District is proud to serve a student population that includes 10.69 percent students with disabilities; when the district's costs to deliver IDEA-required services are not properly funded, it must reallocate money from other programs; and the federal underfunding of IDEA has negatively impacted the academic opportunities of all students for generations, not just those with disabilities.

The operative resolution states: NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the Troy School District Board of Education calls on Congress to immediately pass the IDEA Full Funding Act (S.2217/H.R. 4519), which would create a 10-year mandatory path to fully fund IDEA; and further calls on the state legislature to provide adequate, equitable, and sustainable funding increases to districts to mitigate the harm caused by decades of underfunded schools.

The Troy School District Middle School Curriculum Guide for 2024-2025 is a planning document for students and families that lays out the philosophy, goals, student outcomes, and course structure of the district's middle school program (grades 6-8). The extracted text is truncated partway through the Grade 6 course listings.

Philosophy: Troy middle schools state a commitment to an environment that recognizes, accepts, respects, and meets the diverse needs of young adolescents, pairing academic excellence with developmental responsiveness. The program is characterized as research-based, challenging, integrative, and exploratory, built on a shared educational vision and a cooperative partnership with parents and community.

Goals: Nine goals are listed - that all programs be developmentally appropriate (Goal 1); meet the needs of a diverse student population (Goal 2); ensure development of skills and knowledge in core subjects (Goal 3); help students discover interests, aptitudes, and abilities (Goal 4); provide diversified cultural, social, civic, vocational, and recreational experiences (Goal 5); provide guidance to promote self-esteem, independence, and responsible behavior (Goal 6); establish community partnerships (Goal 7); provide a transition from elementary to high school (Goal 8); and model healthy lifestyles (Goal 9).

Outcomes: The guide commits to preparing each student to become a self-directed learner, a quality worker, a positive communicator, a collaborative and cooperative contributor, and an involved and visionary citizen, each defined by specific traits.

Three-year overview: In 6th grade, all students take five academic classes plus required Physical Education on an every-other-day (EOD) basis, and either music (Band, Orchestra, or Choir, EOD) or Art (EOD). In 7th grade, students take four academic classes plus required Health/Physical Education (half year) and Digital Applications 1.0 (half year); music students take one full-year music course (Concert Band, Chamber Orchestra, or Choir), while non-music students take a total of one full year of electives. In 8th grade, students take four academic classes plus either a full-year music course (Symphonic Band, Advanced Orchestra, or Choir) or, for non-music students, a total of two full-year elective classes.

Course descriptions: The Grade 6 section begins with ELA 6 (full year, required), covering literature of various genres and informational text with emphasis on comprehension of complex texts, textual evidence, theme and character development, and academic vocabulary; and Language Arts 6 (full year, required), covering narrative, informational, and argumentative writing. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A slide presentation titled 'Career Readiness and Technical Education,' delivered at the Troy School District Board of Education Workshop on March 4, 2025. It lays out the district's vision for a continuous K-12 career-readiness pathway, explicitly tied to the district's 'Portrait of a Learner,' and organized into three developmental stages that move students from awareness through exploration to preparation.

Career Awareness (Grades K-5) - 'Let the Journey Begin.' The presentation argues that early career awareness helps students develop a sense of self, discover personal interests and strengths, and explore the world of work beyond jobs held by family members, while building confidence and challenging job stereotypes. Best practices include familiarizing students and families with the six Michigan Career Zones, connecting academic content to those zones across the curriculum, and providing family-engagement opportunities (with resources such as K-1 and 2-5 Career Zone slides, a coloring example, and videos). Current practices: students initiate Educational Development Plans (EDPs) in 1st grade and revise them annually through Media; initiate Talent Portfolios in 3rd grade; participate in intentional career-readiness projects, a STEMi Mobile Field Trip for 4th and 5th graders, Parent Nights, and grade-level career awareness events with guest speakers and assemblies. Future growth focuses on more ways to familiarize students and parents with the six Career Zones and additional family engagement.

Career Exploration (Grades 6-8) - 'The Journey Continues.' Framed as a bridge, middle school is presented as the ideal time for self-discovery and experiential learning, allowing students to consider possible future roles rather than locking in a specific career. Best practices include introducing Michigan's 17 Career Clusters, connecting academics to those clusters, acquiring career/postsecondary/employment knowledge, and continuing to revise the EDP and Talent Portfolio. Current practices: continuation of EDPs and Talent Portfolios, an 8th-grade Parent Night for the middle-to-high-school transition, career-readiness activities embedded in general-education courses, career-exploration electives, and a culminating 8th-grade interview. Future growth includes pacing plans to transition students from Zones to Clusters, cluster-specific field trips, industry tours and job shadows, engagement with guest speakers, visits to high school CTE programs, review of career electives for alignment with high school pathways, and adding EDP and Portrait of a Learner components to 8th-grade interviews.

Career Preparation (Grades 9-12) - 'Multiple Pathways Ahead!' In high school, students update self-assessments, refine evolving career goals, and shift to a more focused pathway aligned with their aspirations, researching labor-market demand and postsecondary opportunities while building pathway-specific and employability skills and cultivating a Talent Portfolio to showcase proficiencies, certifications, experiences and accomplishments. Best practices include in-depth exploration of Michigan career clusters and related pathways, demonstrating career-ready practices (soft skills), revising the EDP annually into a four-year plan, and recording accomplishments in the Talent Portfolio for prospective employers or admissions committees. Current practices note that students review and revise their EDP each year with the help of counselors and a Career Facilitator. (The extracted text ends mid-slide within the Career Preparation section.)

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: The Troy School District's "Guiding Principles for Furniture in Future-Ready Learning Environments" is a one-page framework defining what classroom furniture should accomplish. It organizes goals into five themes: furniture that supports movement and motion, inspires student agency and healthy risk-taking, is comfortable and fosters belonging, meets the needs of all students and staff, and encourages innovative pedagogy. Each theme is expanded with five supporting criteria intended to guide furniture selection for flexible, student-centered classrooms.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A one-page district framework titled "TSD Guiding Principles for Furniture in Future-Ready Learning Environments," establishing criteria to guide classroom furniture selection.

Five guiding principles
- Supports movement and motion: moves easily around the room, partners with other pieces for multiple configurations, encourages students to move, lets them find comfortable proximity to others, and aids efficient transitions.
- Supports and inspires student agency and healthy risk-taking: supports self-awareness and learning needs, can be used in many (even unexpected) ways, increases sustained engagement, empowers students to show their work, and supports organization and access to tools.
- Comfortable and fosters a sense of belonging: gives students a feeling of safety, is comfortable for most, empowers students to organize furniture purposefully, makes the space feel exciting and joyful, and supports a variety of postures.
- Meets the needs of all students and staff: promotes community ("not mine but ours"), supports bodies of all sizes and abilities, creates a positive sensory experience, facilitates teachers working alongside students, and is adjustable on demand.
- Encourages and supports innovative pedagogy: enables whole-group instruction, choice in partner and individual work, small-group gathering and collaboration, and elicits student voice and idea-sharing.

Purpose
Provides a shared, student-centered rubric for evaluating and purchasing flexible furniture as the district develops "future-ready" learning environments. Included as agenda item 8.C. at the March 18, 2025 regular meeting.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A single-page guiding-principles document, "TSD Guiding Principles for Furniture in Future-Ready Learning Environments," setting out the Troy School District's criteria for selecting classroom furniture that supports flexible, student-centered instruction. The framework is organized into five principles, each with five supporting statements.

Furniture that supports movement and motion: has the ability to move around the room easily; partners with other furniture pieces to support multiple configurations; encourages students to move their bodies; allows students to find a comfortable proximity to others; and aides efficient transitions.

Furniture that supports and inspires student agency and healthy risk-taking: supports self-awareness in students and is chosen to support learning needs; can be used by students in many different, even unexpected, ways; increases students' ability to sustain engagement; empowers students to show their work; and supports students in their organization and access to tools.

Furniture that is comfortable and fosters a sense of belonging: allows students a feeling of safety; is considered comfortable by most; empowers students to work together to organize the furniture in a purposeful way; makes the space feel exciting and joyful; and supports a variety of student postures.

Furniture that meets the needs of all students and staff: promotes a sense of community, framed as "not mine but ours"; supports bodies of all sizes and abilities; creates a positive sensory experience; facilitates teachers working alongside students; and is adjustable on-demand.

Furniture that encourages and supports innovative pedagogy: provides access to whole-group instruction; offers choice in partner work; offers choice in individual worktime; enables small-group gathering and collaboration; and elicits student voice and the sharing of ideas.

The document contains no dollar amounts, vendor names, or specific product selections; it functions as a values statement and evaluation rubric to guide future furniture purchases as the district develops "future-ready" learning environments. It was included in the March 18, 2025 regular Board of Education meeting materials as agenda item 8.C.

The item notes that April has been designated as Autism Acceptance Month and that the Troy School District recognizes the need for public awareness to promote acceptance, celebrate differences, and be more inclusive toward autistic individuals. In honor of the month, the Board of Education proposed to pass a resolution celebrating the contributions of all neurodiverse people and working toward ending disparities. The recommended action was to read and adopt the resolution, which includes blank lines for the moving and supporting board members and for the Yes and No vote counts.

The resolution's recitals state: WHEREAS Autism Spectrum Disorder affects more than five million people in the United States; WHEREAS the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report that 1 in 36 children may have autism; WHEREAS autism is a neurological and developmental disorder characterized by social impairment and restricted interactive and communication behaviors, and can affect anyone regardless of race, ethnicity, gender, or socioeconomic background; WHEREAS symptoms and characteristics of autism may present in a variety of combinations and can result in significant, lifelong challenges in areas affecting learning, daily living, employment, social-interactive behaviors, and understanding verbal and nonverbal communications; WHEREAS physicians, psychologists, behavior analysts, speech and language pathologists, occupational therapists, vocational rehabilitation professionals, and educators can assist persons with autism and their families by supporting early identification, education, intervention, recreation, and other opportunities vital to enhanced development and well-being; and WHEREAS the Troy School District is honored to celebrate the many ways individuals with autism enhance the quality of its school community and is committed to fostering acceptance and a sense of belonging as it works to create a more welcoming and inclusive environment for all.

The resolution concludes: NOW, BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED, that the Board of Education hereby recognizes April 2025 as Autism Acceptance Month in the Troy School District.

The five guiding principles
- Supports movement and motion: furniture that moves easily, partners with other pieces for multiple configurations, encourages students to move, lets them find comfortable proximity to others, and aids efficient transitions.
- Supports and inspires student agency and healthy risk-taking: builds self-awareness, can be used in many (even unexpected) ways, sustains engagement, empowers students to show their work, and supports organization and access to tools.

- Meets the needs of all students and staff: promotes community ("not 'mine' but 'ours'"), supports bodies of all sizes and abilities, creates a positive sensory experience, lets teachers work alongside students, and is adjustable on demand.
- Encourages and supports innovative pedagogy: enables whole-group instruction, choice in partner work, choice in individual work time, small-group gathering and collaboration, and elicits student voice.

- Provides the shared standards behind the district's furniture pilots and purchases for "future-ready" learning environments.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
"TSD Guiding Principles for Furniture in Future-Ready Learning Environments" is a single-page criteria framework adopted by the Troy School District (TSD) to guide the selection of classroom furniture. It was included in the April 22, 2025 Regular Meeting of the Board of Education agenda as item 8.C, accompanying the district's Smith Middle School furniture pilot recommendation. The document organizes furniture evaluation around five guiding principles, each with five supporting descriptors.

1. Furniture that supports movement and motion: it should allow students to move around the room easily; partner with other furniture pieces to support multiple configurations; encourage students to move their bodies; allow students to find a comfortable proximity to others; and aid efficient transitions.

2. Furniture that supports and inspires student agency and healthy risk-taking: it should support self-awareness, chosen to meet learning needs; be usable by students in many different and even unexpected ways; increase students' ability to sustain engagement; empower students to show their work; and support students' organization and access to tools.

3. Furniture that is comfortable and fosters a sense of belonging: it should give students a feeling of safety; be considered comfortable by most; empower students to work together to organize the furniture purposefully; make the space feel exciting and joyful; and support a variety of student postures.

4. Furniture that meets the needs of all students and staff: it should promote a sense of community - "not 'mine' but 'ours'"; support bodies of all sizes and abilities; create a positive sensory experience; facilitate teachers working alongside students; and be adjustable on demand.

5. Furniture that encourages and supports innovative pedagogy: it should provide access to whole-group instruction; choice in partner work; choice in individual work time; small-group gathering and collaboration; and elicit student voice and the sharing of ideas.

The principles function as shared standards informing the district's furniture pilots and purchases as it develops "future-ready" learning environments, including the Learning Studios and Learning Commons referenced in related Smith Middle School planning. The document contains no dollar figures, vendors, or votes; it is a qualitative rubric rather than a financial or action item.

Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Pagel, Griffor, Malutan, and Trudel. Two members of the audience attended. A Public Communication period is noted.

The retreat centered on budget planning under Business Services, with four listed items: the Budget; a General Fund Amendment Update (a mid-year revision to the current-year budget); Proposed 2025/26 Expenditures and Revenues (the initial framing of the next fiscal year's budget); and a Budget Building Overview. An "Other" section is also noted on the agenda.

The meeting was adjourned at 10:59 a.m. The minutes were respectfully submitted by Emina Alic, Secretary of the Troy Board of Education (notation EA/jh). As a retreat (study session), the minutes record discussion topics rather than formal motions or vote outcomes.
